articles.title: Medical Devices; Immunology and Microbiology Devices; Classification of the High Throughput DNA Sequencing for Hereditary Cancer Predisposition Assessment Test System
articles.summary: The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) is classifying the high throughput DNA sequencing for hereditary cancer predisposition assessment test system into class II (special controls). The special controls that apply to the device type are identified in this order and will be part of the codified language for classification of the high throughput DNA sequencing for hereditary cancer predisposition assessment test system. We are taking this action because we have determined that classifying the device into class II will provide a reasonable assurance of the safety and effectiveness of the device. We believe this action will also enhance patients' access to beneficial innovative devices, in part by reducing regulatory burdens.

articles.content: Hurricane Isaias: Category 3 Threat to Gulf & Supply Chain - FreightWaves Hurricane Isaias is intensifying in the Gulf, threatening to become a Category 3 storm and unleash significant damage across the Southeast. We break down the storm’s projected path, its potential impact on critical infrastructure like refineries and ports, and what freight and logistics operators can expect for trucking capacity and diesel prices. Stay ahead of the storm’s supply chain disruptions with our full analysis. Hurricane Isaias, currently a Category 1 storm, is forecast to strengthen to a Category 2 by Wednesday and potentially reach Category 3 with winds of up to 100 miles per hour before making landfall Friday around 2 p.m., according to a FreightWaves Sonar analysis. The storm’s projected path stretches from just east of Houston across to the Florida Panhandle, encompassing major freight corridors and energy infrastructure in the Gulf Coast region. The most consequential supply chain risk lies in the energy sector. Up to six refineries sit in the storm’s path, and Gulf State refineries collectively account for 50% of the nation’s refining capacity — a total of 18.2 million barrels per day. Offshore production operators are already sending home nonessential workers, though output continues normally for now. articles.content: Sanctioned 22-Year-Old Tanker Makes Rare Late-Season Arctic Voyage Oil tanker along Northern Sea Route in July 2025. (Source: Atomflot) Sanctioned 22-Year-Old Tanker Makes Rare Late-Season Arctic Voyage Malte Humpert Total Views: 178 October 7, 2026 A 22-year-old product tanker sanctioned by the European Union is making an unusual late-season voyage along Russia’s Northern Sea Route, highlighting the growing use of older, lower-specification vessels to move petroleum products through the Arctic. The Dakar, a 21,300-dwt oil and chemical products tanker built in 2004, is carrying methyl tert-butyl ether (MTBE), a gasoline additive, and appears to be heading west along Russia’s Arctic coast, according vessel tracking data. The cargo was loaded onto another vessel in China in August before being transferred to Dakar off Yeosu, South Korea, in September. Dakar is not an Arctic-specialist tanker, but vessel data from S&P Global indicates that it does have an ice-class designation. That distinguishes it from non-ice-class tankers, while placing it well below the Arc4 and higher ice-class vessels purpose-built for regular Arctic operations. The distinction is increasingly relevant as Russia’s shadow fleet expands its presence on the Northern Sea Route. articles.content: The Costs You Can't See in Packaged Goods Supply Chains - FreightWaves Packaged goods supply chains are full of examples of exception requests, like when a retailer asks for a custom pack configuration, a key account needs a special label, or a shipment gets rerouted on short notice to hit a delivery window. Those kinds of exceptions aren’t necessarily problems on their own. Exception handling can look like good customer service. But on Oct. 15, FreightWaves and G3 Logistics are asking what happens when you stop counting those requests one at a time and start adding them up. That’s the topic of The Hidden Cost-to-Serve in Packaged Goods: Managing Rework, Specialized Handling, and Operational Exceptions, a free webinar that will dig into the repack jobs, relabeling work, retailer-specific requirements, and expedited changes that accumulate inside packaged goods networks until they’re no longer exceptions at all. Without visibility into what those exceptions cost, they can be devastating to margins over time. G3 Logistics brings transportation, warehousing, and supply chain expertise to a common packaged goods challenge: customer requests that add work beyond the standard flow. A package change, relabeling request, or tighter delivery window can affect handling, schedules, inventory, and capacity across multiple teams. articles.content: JP Morgan-backed NOCC expands China car carrier programme - Splash247 CIMC Raffles JP Morgan-backed Norwegian Car Carriers (NOCC) has expanded its newbuilding programme in China, adding another pair of 7,100 ceu ships at CIMC Raffles. Shipbuilding sources place the latest vessels at the group’s Yantai Raffles facility for delivery in 2030, extending a relationship that has already produced four LNG dual-fuel car carriers for the Oslo-based tonnage provider. The latest pair would take NOCC’s confirmed programme with CIMC Raffles to six ships. However, shipbuilding databases seen by Splash indicate the programme could be larger still. In addition to two 7,100 ceu units listed as hulls 641 and 642 for delivery in 2030, the databases show another two ships, hulls 651 and 652, against NOCC for delivery in 2030 and 2031. Those additional two units have not been disclosed by NOCC and could represent options attached to the latest contract. NOCC’s own fleet list has yet to reflect any of the latest additions and currently shows only the four ships from its earlier series. The first two, NOCC Pacific and NOCC Adriatic, have already entered service. CIMC Raffles delivered the latter in January this year. The remaining ships from that original programme, NOCC Kattegat and NOCC Skagerak, are due next year. articles.content: Commodity trader takes Pelagic handysize for up to 11 months - Splash247 Pelagic Partners Cyprus-based shipowner and fund manager Pelagic Partners has fixed its handysize bulker UBC Houston to an unnamed major commodity trader for up to 11 months. The 2015-built, 39,000 dwt vessel has secured a nine-to-11-month time charter at $17,250 per day, Pelagic said. The company did not identify the charterer. The Chengxi Shipyard-built bulker forms part of the Pelagic Yield Fund and trades in the UBC Pool. Pelagic acquired the vessel in June 2023 as part of an expansion of its dry bulk exposure. At the time, the acquisition took the fund compartment holding the ship to seven vessels and Pelagic’s total acquired fleet since inception to 18 units. The latest fixture gives Pelagic medium-term cover while leaving the ship open again next year. At the headline rate, the contract represents roughly $4.7m to $5.8m of gross hire over the nine-to-11-month window before commissions, off-hire and other deductions. Pelagic’s wider shipping investment platform has also been active in dry bulk this year. In July, Oslo-listed Pelagic Credit struck a $47.4m sale-and-leaseback deal covering three Hartmann-controlled handysize bulkers, its first investment in the sector. The ships were placed on seven-year bareboat charters back to Hartmann. Michael Kanko, CEO of ImportGenius.com, explains what this trade data delta signifies for the global supply chain. He details how granular shipping records are used for everything from sourcing new components to ensuring compliance with international sanctions, and why transparency in air cargo data is the next big battle for US manufacturers. ImportGenius has identified a more than $100 billion gap between what China reported shipping to the United States last year and what U.S. records show as received — a discrepancy that highlights the limitations of relying on government trade statistics alone and the growing role of bill-of-lading data in supply chain intelligence. The finding emerged when ImportGenius normalized its shipment-level data into TEUs — the standard 20-foot equivalent unit used in global container trade — and cross-referenced that count against U.S. Census dollar values to derive a value-per-container figure. Comparing that metric to China’s own TEU-normalized figures produced what the company described as a major and “mystifying” difference. The 56-year-old master mariner, founder of ShipGod AI, spends 25 years with China Yangtze Shipping, rising from deck cadet to …
articles.content: ShipGod AI: Why every vessel needs its own digital memory - Splash247 After four decades at sea and ashore, Bing Hou has reached a simple conclusion about shipmanagement: too much of what keeps vessels safe still depends on paper, spreadsheets and what individual seafarers happen to remember. The 56-year-old master mariner, founder of ShipGod AI, spends 25 years with China Yangtze Shipping, rising from deck cadet to Class-1 ocean-going master and serving on everything from containerships and tankers to LNG carriers, passenger ships and offshore vessels. Since 2016, Hou has worked ashore in marine management, ship surveying, DPA roles and teaching. Across all of it, he says one problem keeps resurfacing. “The paper never really changed,” he tells Maritime CEO. “ISM got the principle right decades ago: every ship must operate its own Safety Management System, fitted to that specific ship. But in practice, the documents that keep ships safe still live in binders, spreadsheets and memory.” The result, he argues, is a steady leakage of institutional knowledge. Records are often completed after events, while valuable operating experience can disappear whenever officers sign off. “The turning point for me was watching how much time good officers spend managing documents instead of being officers, and how much of what they know is never captured for the next crew,” Hou says. The platform allows businesses to order from more than 140,000 restaurants nationwide and provides tools for companies to manage ordering and food spending. OK By Oh Seok-min SEOUL, Oct. 8 (Yonhap) -- South Korea is strictly enforcing its export controls on Russia, the foreign ministry said Thursday, stressing that no exports of commercial petroleum products to Russia have been confirmed through customs clearance procedures. Currently, South Korea prohibits exports of strategic items to Russia and subjects an additional 1,402 non-strategic items that could potentially be used for military purposes to case-by-case export authorization, according to the ministry. "The controlled items are determined through interagency discussions after comprehensively considering their potential military use, economic impact and international coordination," the ministry said in an explanatory note jointly issued by the industry ministry and the customs agency. Outbound shipments to Russia dropped to US$4 billion in 2025 from $10 billion in 2021 as South Korea joined international efforts to maintain peace through export controls "despite the economic burden on companies and the public," the ministry noted. articles.content: Fragmented trade drives dry bulk tonne-mile demand - Splash247 Dry bulk shipping has entered the final quarter of 2026 in considerably better shape than most owners expected, with industry leaders at last week’s Splash Singapore conference arguing that increasingly fragmented trade could keep vessel demand elevated even without spectacular growth in cargo volumes. G2 Ocean chief executive Arthur English admitted the strength of the market had surprised him, particularly in minor bulks where underlying tonnes have barely grown. “All of the growth has come from geopolitical disruptions and delays in ports and so on,” English told the Dry Bulk Market Outlook panel. articles.title: New UN data: China widens lead in liner-shipping connectivity
articles.summary:
China pressed its dominance in shipping connectivity while country-level gains and losses became increasingly uneven in the third quarter, a UN report finds.
The post New UN data: China widens lead in liner-shipping connectivity appeared first on FreightWaves.
articles.content: New UN data: China widens lead in liner-shipping connectivity - FreightWaves Promo Code: FALLFORF3 Limited Quantity Available - Join us at F3: Future of Freight Festival, October 27 & 28th Register Now × China’s Liner Shipping Connectivity Index reached 1,347.6 in September 2026, more than double the scores of second-ranked South Korea, at 633.0, and Singapore, at 626.7. The United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD) index gauges a country’s integration into container-shipping networks using factors including vessel calls, port capacity, carrier and service availability, largest ship size and the number of countries reached through direct services. The latest figures underline Asia’s continuing central role in liner shipping. Wholly owned CLC Newbuildings has signed a letter of intent with Hubei Guangji Green Energy Shipbuilding Group covering 10 firm 1,300 teu containerships plus two sets of 10 options. Pricing and delivery dates have not been disclosed. If all the options are taken up, the newbuilding programme alone would exceed Contships’ existing fleet of 27 feeder vessels. The ships will use the new ContshipMax CV1300 design developed with Shanghai Merchant Ship Design and Research Institute (SDARI). Despite the name, capacity is listed at 1,324 teu, including 340 reefer plugs. The conventionally fuelled vessels will feature Tier III Mitsubishi main engines, low-pressure SCR systems, Daihatsu generators, shaft generators and a package of energy-saving devices. Construction will take place at Guangji’s recently commissioned yard at Wuxue on the Yangtze River, with the Chinese builder working in partnership with Shanghai Waigaoqiao Shipbuilding & Offshore Project Management. articles.content: UK Sanctions Five LNG Carriers in New Russia Package LNG carrier Alexey Kosygin. Photo courtesy Zvezda Shipbuilding UK Sanctions Five LNG Carriers in New Russia Package Malte Humpert Total Views: 387 October 1, 2026 The United Kingdom has sanctioned five liquefied natural gas carriers as part of a new package of measures targeting Russia’s efforts to expand a maritime “shadow fleet” for LNG exports, including three Russian-built Arc7 ice-class vessels intended to support the Arctic LNG 2 project. The five LNG carriers named in the Oct. 1 sanctions notice are Chaivo, Portovyy, Aleksey Kosygin, Konstantin Posiet and Pyotr Stolypin. The vessels are subject to UK shipping and trade sanctions that prohibit their operation and chartering, bar them from UK ports and restrict the provision and procurement of a broad range of maritime services. The three newest vessels – Aleksey Kosygin, Konstantin Posyet and Pyotr Stolypin – are part of a series of large high ice-class LNG carriers being built for Russia’s Arctic LNG program. Aleksey Kosygin was delivered in December 2025 while Konstantin Posyet followed in June 2026. Pyotr Stolypin was being prepared for sea trials at the Zvezda shipyard in September, according to Russian state oil company Rosneft. London’s sanctioning of Pyotr Stolypin before entering commercial service is noteworthy. The Australian financial group said the funding was provided to shipowning entities within the Athens-based Technomar Group, although it did not identify the seven vessels, disclose pricing or give the maturity of the facility. The transaction forms part of a growing Greek shipping book at Macquarie, which has deployed more than $2bn in the market since completing its first deal with Atlas Maritime in 2017. Its current Greek shipping portfolio exceeds $1bn across more than 75 transactions. Macquarie has completed more than 25 transactions with Atlas alone and has also been building relationships with newer Greek names. The financier revealed that it backed Adele Shipmanagement’s first bulker acquisitions and now finances four ships for the company. Technomar, established by Youroukos in 1994, remains heavily weighted towards containerships while also managing dry bulk tonnage. Current vessel-registry data links the company to a fleet approaching 100 managed ships. The owner has a long track record of buying secondhand boxships. Splash previously tracked Technomar picking up tonnage from German owners during an earlier phase of container fleet expansion, including a pair of 7,849 teu post-panamaxes acquired from Zeaborn. articles.content: Namura absorbs Imari steel arm ahead of shipbuilding expansion - Splash247 Namura Japan’s Namura Shipbuilding is absorbing its wholly owned Imari Steel Center as the shipbuilder moves to tighten control of production ahead of a major expansion of its newbuilding business. The Osaka-listed builder has approved the merger, with the transaction scheduled to take effect on April 1, 2027. Namura will remain the surviving company and Imari Steel Center will be dissolved. Imari Steel Center sits next to Namura’s main Imari yard in Saga prefecture and handles the upstream steel functions supporting vessel construction, including unloading, sorting, storage, processing and quality assurance of shipbuilding plate. Namura said combining the operations should speed up decision-making, allow better deployment of personnel and other resources, improve manufacturing efficiency and help with recruitment and training as the group increases newbuilding output. The internal reshuffle comes as Namura embarks on one of its biggest capacity pushes in years. Japan’s transport ministry last month approved up to ¥49.9bn ($319m) of government backing for an investment programme involving Namura and subsidiary Hakodate Dock, part of Tokyo’s wider drive to rebuild domestic shipbuilding capacity. Namura is also moving ahead with a new large construction dock, the first major shipbuilding dock to be developed in Japan since Imabari Shipbuilding completed its Marugame facility in 2017. The six MR2s and two LR2s form part of a much wider newbuilding drive that has pushed Advantage’s reported orderbook to 22 ships against 28 tankers currently in operation. articles.content: U-Ming doubles down in China with six-ship bulker spend - Splash247 U-Ming Taiwan’s U-Ming Marine Transport has committed up to $312m on six more bulkers in China, adding four ultramaxes and firming another pair of Newcastlemaxes as it presses ahead with plans to build a 100-ship fleet. Two separate Taiwan exchange disclosures from U-Ming’s Singapore subsidiary put the combined investment at between $296m and $312m. The larger ships are two 211,000 dwt newcastlemaxes at Jiangsu Hantong Ship Heavy Industry, priced at between $77m and $80m each for a total of $154m to $160m. The filing follows U-Ming’s June contract at the same yard for two firm ships plus two options at exactly the same price range. The latest two-ship disclosure matches the optional pair attached to that deal, taking the Hantong programme to four firm units. U-Ming is also paying between $142m and $152m for four 64,000 dwt ultramaxes at Sumec Marine-controlled New Dayang Shipbuilding, equating to $35.5m to $38m per ship. The first of the ultramaxes is scheduled for delivery in the fourth quarter of 2029, with the remaining three following during 2030. The latest contracting advances an expansion plan approved by U-Ming earlier this year covering four 210,000 dwt bulkers and four ultramaxes. Splash first linked the Far Eastern Group-backed owner to the Hantong newcastlemax programme in June, when the initial two-plus-two deal emerged. articles.content: Almi expands China orderbook with three more ultramaxes - Splash247 Almi Marine Greek dry bulk owner Almi Marine Management has added another three ultramax newbuildings in China, expanding a fleet renewal drive that began earlier this year. Greek shipping sources report that the Athens-based owner has booked three 64,000 dwt bulkers at COSCO Shipping Heavy Industry’s Zhoushan yard, with delivery scheduled for 2030. The fresh deal follows Almi’s return to the newbuilding market in February after a four-year absence. Managing director Christos Hadjigeorgiou confirmed at the time that the company had signed for two 64,000 dwt next-generation ultramaxes at Nantong COSCO KHI Ship Engineering, or NACKS, for delivery in the second quarter of 2029. The latest Zhoushan trio takes Almi’s known forward programme to five 64,000 dwt newbuilds across two COSCO-linked yards. The owner already has close ties with the Chinese-Japanese NACKS and DACKS yards, taking three ultramaxes from DACKS in 2024. Almi currently controls six bulkers. Its fleet renewal has also included the disposal of older supramax tonnage, including the 2008-built Anasa. For a price marker, Splash noted in August that Xclusiv was assessing a standard Chinese-built ultramax at around $36m, which would put three ships at roughly $108m if Almi contracted near prevailing levels. The actual price has not been disclosed. TagsGreece Adis AjdinOctober 5, 2026 0 32 1 minute read Follow Us Facebook X LinkedIn Tumblr Pinterest Red

The Tianjin-based offshore engineering contractor said it had successfully bid for the Maydan Mahzam EPIC2 package, covering engineering, procurement, construction, and installation work. The scope includes more than 100 km of subsea pipelines, cables, and umbilicals, along with associated offshore infrastructure. The package forms part of QatarEnergy’s wider redevelopment of the mature Maydan Mahzam oil field. The latest award follows another large Maydan Mahzam contract handed to PetroVietnam Technical Services Corporation (PTSC) in September. QatarEnergy selected PTSC for an EPIC package covering design, procurement, construction, transportation, offshore installation, connection, commissioning, modification and upgrading work across the field cluster. PTSC has not officially disclosed the contract value, although Vietnamese media reports put it at around $3bn. Maydan Mahzam is located around 110 km northeast of mainland Qatar and has been producing since 1965. articles.content: Oil exports surge back through Hormuz despite mounting attacks - Splash247 IMO Oil flows from the Middle East have climbed back above pre-war levels even as attacks on tankers around the Strait of Hormuz accelerate to their fastest pace since the conflict with Iran erupted on February 28. Provisional Kpler data shows regional crude exports exceeded pre-war volumes on four days during the final week of September, reaching between 19.5m and 22.5m barrels per day. The seven-day moving average stood at 18.5m barrels per day on October 1, compared with an average of around 18m barrels per day in the year before the war. The numbers cover Hormuz and Red Sea movements as well as terminal exports and ship-to-ship transfers in the Gulf of Oman. LNG cargoes exiting Hormuz also rose in September to their highest monthly level since February. The recovery is providing a powerful cargo base for tanker markets, although brokers caution that improving logistics could eventually erode some of the extraordinary inefficiencies that have propelled rates. “For dirty tankers, higher Gulf crude exports and the return of Yanbu provide firm underlying cargo demand,” Sentosa Shipbrokers noted, adding that more efficient logistics could gradually reduce STS activity and unwind part of the “exceptional inefficiency premium” supporting VLCC earnings. articles.content: Japan targets 35 shadow fleet ships in first vessel sanctions - Splash247 Greenpeace Japan has imposed sanctions directly on individual vessels for the first time, targeting 35 ships linked to Russia’s shadow fleet as Tokyo steps up efforts to restrict Moscow’s oil-export network. The measures took effect on October 2 under Japan’s Foreign Exchange and Foreign Trade Act. Japanese companies will now need government permission to provide specified services to the 35 vessels and for capital transactions, including loans and debt guarantees, connected with their sale, purchase, lease or charter. Japan’s foreign ministry has identified all 35 ships by IMO number. A limited transition applies to contracts concluded before October 2, but only where the relevant obligations or services are completed before November 1. The restrictions cover services including ship repairs and insurance. It is the first time Tokyo has placed vessels themselves under sanctions, bringing Japan closer to the approach already adopted by the UK and European Union against ageing tankers moving Russian oil outside mainstream Western shipping, finance and insurance channels. The shipping measures formed part of a wider package that also froze the assets of 33 Russian organisations and nine individuals and introduced export restrictions against four entities in Turkey and the UAE. articles.content: Chevron extends Australia asset-integrity deal with EnerMech - Splash247 Chevron UK oilfield services specialist EnerMech has secured a five-year extension to its non-destructive testing contract with Chevron Australia, retaining the inspection and asset-integrity work until the end of 2031. The Aberdeen-headquartered services company first won the assignment in 2017. The renewed agreement covers inspection and integrity support across Chevron Australia’s operations, including major LNG assets in Western Australia. Financial terms were not disclosed. EnerMech has supported Chevron on the Gorgon and Wheatstone LNG projects through commissioning, maintenance, shutdown campaigns, and continuing operational work. Its scope includes advanced non-destructive testing, condition monitoring, corrosion-management services, statutory inspections, engineering support, and specialist integrity work. The extension comes as LNG operators continue to focus on maintaining availability and managing ageing equipment within complex export facilities. Gorgon, located on Barrow Island, and Wheatstone, near Onslow, are among Australia’s largest LNG developments. EnerMech provides a wider range of Australian services across process, pipeline and subsea operations, cranes and lifting, hydraulics, valves, electrical and instrumentation, and integrity management.
